summary: The note is a Sydney Morning Herald market report saying the ASX is set to rise after US shares surged on hopes the Federal Reserve is done raising interest rates, following a weaker-than-expected US jobs report. It covers Wall Street's weekly gains, falling Treasury yields, and an Australian session in which energy and industrials lagged while banks rebounded on Westpac's trading update. It also includes analyst views on the Reserve Bank's Tuesday rate decision and consumer confidence.
one_line: ASX set to rise after Wall Street rallied on hopes the Fed has finished hiking rates, with Westpac lifting banks and energy stocks lagging.
key_facts: The S&P 500 climbed 40.56 points on Friday, or 0.9 per cent, to 4,358.3.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 222.24, or 0.7 per cent, to 34,061.32, and the Nasdaq composite jumped 184.09, or 1.4 per cent, to 13,478.28.
A US jobs report showed employers hired fewer workers last month than economists expected, easing inflation pressure, with average hourly earnings rising less in October than expected.
The 10-year Treasury yield eased to 4.52 per cent from 4.67 per cent late Thursday, and from more than five per cent last week, when it hit its highest level since 2007.
The Fed's main interest rate is above 5.25 per cent, its highest level since 2001.
Generac soared nearly 28 per cent for its best week since its stock began trading in 2010, and Expedia Group rose nearly 22 per cent for its best week since early 2020.
Apple fell 0.5 per cent despite stronger quarterly profit, as investors were likely disappointed with its revenue forecast for the last three months of 2023.
Energy companies fell one per cent on the ASX, with Woodside down 0.8 per cent, Santos down 0.4 per cent, Ampol down 1.2 per cent, Yancoal down 1.7 per cent and Whitehaven down 2 per cent.
Lynas Rare Earths, down 3.1 per cent, was the biggest large-cap decliner; Computershare fell 2.9 per cent, Seven West Holdings 1.9 per cent and Worley 1.3 per cent.
TMS Capital's Ben Clark said Westpac's better-than-expected trading update led a resurgence in banks and set the tone for NAB and ANZ results due in the next week.
Clark said the market moved from pricing an 80 per cent chance of a rate rise on Tuesday to 50-50.
CreditorWatch chief economist Anneke Thompson said another cash rate increase on Tuesday would be "the nail in the coffin for consumer confidence".
Traders are moving up expectations for the first Fed rate cut, potentially by the summer, according to CME Group data.
